props.title: The Roaring Twenties
props.initialSlug: WWI vet turns bootlegger in gangster epic

sections.content: The Roaring Twenties (1939) stands as Warner Bros' definitive gangster swan song to the Prohibition era, bridging Pre-Code gangster films like Little Caesar (1931) and The Public Enemy (1931) with the more complex crime dramas that would follow. James Cagney delivers a masterful performance as Eddie Bartlett, a WWI veteran who turns to bootlegging when legitimate opportunities dry up. Unlike earlier gangster protagonists, Eddie isn't inherently criminal - he's a victim of circumstance, representing thousands of returning veterans who found an changed America waiting for them.

sections.content: Director Raoul Walsh crafts a sophisticated narrative that doubles as social commentary. The film's documentary-style opening and newsreel footage ground the story in historical reality, while the rise-and-fall structure became a template for later crime epics like Goodfellas (1990) and Once Upon a Time in America (1984). Humphrey Bogart's portrayal of the ruthless George Hally provides a darker contrast to Cagney's more sympathetic Eddie, highlighting the film's exploration of how different men responded to the era's moral chaos.

The film's technical achievements are remarkable for 1939. Ernest Haller's cinematography captures both the glittering nightclub scenes and shadowy street violence with equal skill. The memorable finale, with Eddie dying on the snow-covered steps of a church, influenced countless crime films that followed, including White Heat (1949) and The Godfather (1972). Priscilla Lane and Gladys George provide strong supporting performances that elevate the film beyond simple gangster thrills. SUBHEAD: Impact on Crime Cinema

sections.content: The Roaring Twenties marked a crucial evolution in crime films, moving away from simple morality tales toward more nuanced examinations of society's role in creating criminals. This approach influenced post-war noir like Force of Evil (1948) and contemporary crime dramas like Miller's Crossing (1990). The film's structure - using a narrator and historical footage to contextualize its story - anticipated docudrama techniques used decades later in films like Bonnie and Clyde (1967).
